Series::LinearAlgAccessor::slogdet¶

Back to Series::LinearAlgAccessor API Reference

Signatures¶

Series Series::LinearAlgAccessor::slogdet() const
Series SeriesLinearAlgProxy::slogdet() const

What It Does¶

slogdet() decomposes each determinant into sign and logarithmic magnitude:

slogdet(A) = [sign(det(A)), log(abs(det(A)))]

It returns both values in one Series. The final output dimension has length two:

result[..., 0] = sign
result[..., 1] = log-absolute-determinant

This representation retains orientation while keeping determinant magnitude in a logarithmic range.

Separating Orientation From Magnitude¶

A real determinant contains two distinct pieces of information. Its sign says whether the transformation preserves or reverses orientation. Its magnitude says how strongly area or volume is scaled. Logging the magnitude makes very large and very small scales manageable, while storing sign separately avoids asking the real logarithm to represent a negative number.

The original determinant can be reconstructed conceptually as

det(A) = sign * exp(logabsdet)

For singular matrices, the pair is [0, -inf]. In the limiting expression, exp(-inf) is zero, and the zero sign clearly marks the loss of invertibility.

Shape Contract¶

Input shape

Output shape

Layout

[n, n]

[2]

[sign, logabsdet]

[b, n, n]

[b, 2]

one pair per matrix

[..., n, n]

[..., 2]

batch shape followed by pair axis

Unlike det() and logdet(), the result is not rank zero for one matrix. The two matrix dimensions are replaced by a final length-two result dimension.

Returns¶

Series A single Series whose last dimension stores sign at index 0 and log-absolute-determinant at index 1.

For real input, sign is `1`, `-1`, or `0`. The log-magnitude is finite for
a nonsingular finite matrix and `-inf` for a singular matrix.

Gradient¶

The sign output is treated as piecewise constant. The differentiable log-magnitude output has the same local derivative as logdet() away from singular matrices:

d log(abs(det(A))) / dA = A^-T

If the incoming sensitivity along the final result axis is [g_sign, g_log], only g_log contributes:

dL/dA = g_log A^-T

This makes select(..., 1) the natural scalar objective when differentiating the log-magnitude of one matrix.

Examples¶

Example 1. A positive determinant produces positive sign and its logarithmic magnitude.

auto matrix = pluss::make_series({{4.0, 7.0}, {2.0, 6.0}});
std::cout << matrix.linearalg.slogdet() << "\n";

The determinant is 10, so the pair is [1, log(10)].

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 2.3025851]

Example 2. Row exchange changes only the sign component.

auto original = pluss::make_series({{4.0, 7.0}, {2.0, 6.0}});
auto swapped = pluss::make_series({{2.0, 6.0}, {4.0, 7.0}});

std::cout << "original=" << original.linearalg.slogdet() << "\n";
std::cout << "swapped=" << swapped.linearalg.slogdet() << "\n";

Both determinants have magnitude 10.

Output¶

original=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[1, 2.3025851]
swapped=pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[-1, 2.3025851]

Example 3. Singular input has zero sign and negative-infinite log-magnitude.

auto singular = pluss::make_series({{1.0, 2.0}, {2.0, 4.0}});
std::cout << singular.linearalg.slogdet() << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2], strides=[1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=2, contiguous=true)
data=[0, -inf]

Example 4. Batched input appends a pair axis after the batch axis.

auto batch = pluss::make_series({
    {{1.0, 0.0}, {0.0, 3.0}},
    {{2.0, 1.0}, {1.0, 2.0}},
    {{1.0, 2.0}, {2.0, 4.0}},
});

std::cout << batch.linearalg.slogdet() << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[3,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=6, contiguous=true)
data=[[1, 1.0986123],
  [1, 1.0986123],
  [0, -inf]]

The first axis still identifies the three input matrices. The final axis now selects sign or log-magnitude.

Example 5. Select the log-magnitude slot before reverse mode for one matrix.

auto matrix = pluss::make_series({{2.0, 0.0}, {0.0, 4.0}});
matrix.tracks_slope_(true);

matrix.linearalg.slogdet().select(0, 1).reverse();

std::cout << matrix.sensitivity() << "\n";

The selected slot is log(abs(det(A))); its derivative is A^-T.

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[2,2], strides=[2,1], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=4, contiguous=true)
data=[[0.5, 0],
  [-0, 0.25]]

Example 6. Reconstruct a moderate determinant by indexing the two result slots. This is useful when the ordinary-scale value is genuinely needed.

auto matrix = pluss::make_series({{2.0, 6.0}, {4.0, 7.0}});
auto signed_log = matrix.linearalg.slogdet();
auto reconstructed = signed_log.select(0, 0).mul(
    signed_log.select(0, 1).exp());

std::cout << reconstructed << "\n";

Output¶

pluss::Series(shape=[], strides=[], dtype=float64, platform=cpu, numel=1, contiguous=true)
data=-10

Gotchas And Failure Modes¶

  • slogdet() returns one Series, not a pair of C++ objects.

  • The last output dimension is always the [sign, logabsdet] axis. For a batched result, select along that final dimension rather than batch dimension zero.

  • Singular input returns [0, -inf]; reconstructing with ordinary arithmetic should account for the zero sign explicitly.

  • The sign slot does not contribute a reverse sensitivity. The log-magnitude derivative is undefined at singular matrices.

  • Input must end in square matrix dimensions.

Summary¶

slogdet() preserves determinant orientation and logarithmic magnitude in one [..., 2] result. Index 0 is sign, index 1 is log-magnitude, and only the log-magnitude slot contributes the inverse-transpose gradient.
